claims.text: Element segregation at grain boundaries is the primary governor of toughness retention or loss in HEAs under demanding conditions.
Grain-boundary segregation alters local cohesion and promotes intergranular fracture during mechanical or thermal loading.
The initial HEA is near-homogeneous and single-phase, with minimal segregation and uniform elemental distributions at grain boundaries.
Controlled annealing followed by fast versus slow cooling can selectively vary grain-boundary chemistry.
In-situ elevated-temperature SEM or TEM fracture experiments can monitor crack propagation while thermal history is varied.
Temperatures of 600–1000 °C are representative of severe HEA service environments.
Elevated temperature combined with slow strain-rate or sustained loading facilitates grain-boundary segregation and embrittlement.
Time- and temperature-dependent diffusion causes local enrichment of selected elements at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary elemental enrichment increases susceptibility to intergranular cracking.
Thermally driven segregation of embrittling elements reduces grain-boundary cohesive strength, promotes intergranular crack nucleation and propagation, and lowers toughness.
Slower cooling promotes increased grain-boundary segregation.
Higher annealing temperatures promote increased grain-boundary segregation and consequent toughness loss.
Relative to a fast-quenched or homogenized baseline, slowly cooled or more highly annealed samples will have lower fracture energy and a shift from transgranular to intergranular fracture.
A homogenized alloy with minimal grain-boundary segregation has comparatively higher toughness and predominantly transgranular fracture at moderate service temperatures.
The proposed mechanism applies mainly to single-phase or near-single-phase HEAs under time and temperature regimes permitting appreciable elemental diffusion.
The mechanism should become less important at very low temperatures or in alloys with negligible grain-boundary diffusivity.
Short-range order, nanoscale precipitation, and dislocation substructures may also modulate toughness loss.

If enhanced grain-boundary segregation does not significantly reduce toughness or increase intergranular cracking under matched loading, and minimally segregated specimens embrittle similarly, the segregation-driven mechanism is refuted.
